Tech Report: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Sources indicate that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

It has been revealed that “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell claims. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

According to recent reports, the screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics firm. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

According to recent reports, for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

Recent findings suggest that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Industry observers note that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

It has been revealed that sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team highlighted me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

Industry observers note that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga states, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

Sources indicate that about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga claims. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Industry observers note that dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Sources indicate that remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics firm XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

Recent findings suggest that “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” states Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Sources indicate that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson indicates. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more key than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

Industry observers note that during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” states neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

In a recent development, medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

According to recent reports, but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, states experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

According to recent reports, and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” claims neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

It has been revealed that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

Sources indicate that “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra claims. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

In a recent development, if smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Sources indicate that neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

According to recent reports, in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell indicates. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in upcoming funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Sources indicate that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga claims they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

Industry observers note that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print problem as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when comparing free weights and gym machines, I am firmly on the side of free weights. Equipment like dumbbells and kettlebells allows you to work both sides of your body independently, while using barbells means you can load heavy, working your core muscles harder to stabilize you without the help and support of a machine.

There are other benefits, too, like building stability, coordination, balance and range of motion, but I use certain gym machines like cables or leg presses, and I may start a beginner on certain machines until they feel more confident with the movements.

All of this is to say, there's one piece of equipment I avoid for core exercises, particularly sit-ups, because more often than not, I see people in the gym getting injured.

Read on for the full lowdown, and what to do instead.

Recent findings suggest that the GHD machine, or Glute Ham Developer as it was originally designed, can be used (and is commonly used) for sit-ups. The GHD sit-up is an intense sit-up variation used to improve core strength, stability and hip mobility, as it requires excessive and full range of motion as you lean back.

Although your hip flexors help power the torso upward, they shouldn't take over the exercise, which targets the abs running along the front of your stomach. The problem is, the excessive range of motion can load the lower back, and if you don't perform the exercise properly, with enough core engagement, or if you currently have a health condition (like high or low blood pressure), are pre- or post-natal, or have an injury, this exercise promptly becomes contraindicated.

For this reason, I skip the GHD machine for core exercises, especially for beginners, as repeated lumbar flexion and extension of the spine in an unsupported position offers more problems, in my opinion, than benefits.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Here's what I recommend instead.

You need a lot of power to drive your body to a sitting position, so the first thing I'll do is get someone on a pull-up bar for hanging leg raises or knee tucks. L-sits are also a great option for developing deep core strength while also targeting the hip flexors and grip strength.

Although your back is still unsupported, you're putting a lot less strain on your spine while still building strength in your upper body.

It has been revealed that if you're determined to use a GHD machine, I recommend relearning to brace your core using my five-minute bracing routine. Core engagement isn't just about squeezing your stomach hard or sucking your belly in; it's about gently bracing the abdomen and bearing down, as if someone is about to punch you in the gut. You'll also need to exhale as your body meets the most resistance, which means as you sit up in this case.

Finally, did you know your diaphragm is a core muscle? Breathing properly requires diaphragmatic breathing, which means directing your breath downward rather than out through your chest.

I strongly recommend spending some time activating your core and diaphragm first, and trying some pelvic tilts to get everything fired up beforehand while supporting your spine.

If possible, I would use dumbbells, Bosu trainers, resistance bands, kettlebells, or Swiss balls over going anywhere near the GHD machine.

You can slowly overload the body as you get stronger, adding weight or volume as you develop core strength and stability. Bosu trainers test balance and stability, and kettlebells increase range of motion as you can move them more freely.

In a recent development, free weights are also far more functional than many gym machines, as you teach your muscles to support you rather than relying on a piece of kit. This is extremely beneficial for your core, which in turn is better for your back health.

It has been revealed that movements that are functional should also feel natural, aiding everyday activities. Plus, you should feel like you have far more control.

You put a lot of trust into the GHD when doing one of these sit-ups. Your entire body is held by the two rollers that clamp around your feet. It's not for everyone.

There's an extensive library of exercises that benefit your body more, and it's a great opportunity to experiment with what does and doesn't work for your body.

I would start with these 5 Pilates exercises and some lower abs workouts.

I also really rate endurance-focused core exercises that use isometric contraction, which means you hold tension in the working muscles without them lengthening or shortening. Examples include the hollow hold (pictured above) and plank variations.

In a recent development, I don't know many people who get away with zero pain using the GHD machine, and it might be a lack of core engagement, weakness in the stabilizing muscles, existing back pain, poor technique, or something as simple as body mechanics. For me, I just don't think it's worth the risk.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This shift changes how devices are designed.
  • It has been revealed that this White Paper explains these challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

It has been revealed that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home.
  • HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.
  • Sources indicate that A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home. The only carve-out is lighting, because some rooms are hard to judge by time of day alone. Depending on the windows and placement against the sun, some rooms might need light-based automations earlier in the day than others. The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes that with a light sensor most motion sensors lack, along with mmWave radar.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Sources indicate that A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations. If you’re still for long periods, you’re invisible, and the automation assumes the room is empty. The Lafaer LWR02 pairs PIR with 2.4 GHz mmWave radar. The PIR-based motion sees you walking in, and the radar sees the minor stuff, like breathing and shifting on the couch, so the room stays “occupied” for as long as you are in it. The two together also reduce false positives from ceiling fans, curtains, and the dog, because the radar and PIR both must agree before the sensor reports motion.

In Apple Home, that indicates up as an occupancy sensor and a motion sensor from the same device.

“Turn on the lights when someone enters” is a common automation I use, but it can be tricky. What if you only want it when it’s not light outside? Doing it based on time of day sometimes works, but what about depending on where the windows are facing, etc.? You might have a room that gets darker an hour earlier than another room. “Turn on the lights when someone enters, and it’s dark in the room” is what the light sensor can handle for you.

Industry observers note that in the Home app, that means triggering a sensor for occupancy, then converting the automation into a Shortcut and adding a condition for the light level. It’s a few extra steps, but it does really give you more fine control over how it works.

Presence, motion, light, temperature, and humidity all come from the same device, and each one appears in Apple Home as its own sensor, so you can build automations around whichever ones fit the room.

It has been revealed that it’s IPX3-rated, so bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms are fine to use in. Coverage is about 13 feet for presence and 26 for motion across about 120 degrees, which works in a bedroom, office, or bathroom. It’s not going to cover a great room from one corner. The base is a magnetic half sphere, so you can aim it, and it mounts with adhesive or sits on a shelf. I generally like to use the shelf for these types of sensors.

The Lafaer LWR02 is Matter over Thread, so it pairs directly with a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K with no Lafaer hub or account needed. It runs on two included AAA batteries, is rated for up to two years, and rechargeable AAAs work with it as well. Thread is why a sensor doing this much can last that long on batteries. All sensor data is processed locally, so it only uses a trickle on the batteries.

It has been revealed that lights that turn off while you’re sitting still in the room are the reason a lot of people stop using motion automations in smart homes. The Lafaer LWR02 fixes that with mmWave radar and then lets you have more granular control of light-based automations based on what’s actually in the environment in the room, not just the time of day.

The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor is available on Amazon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taiwan’s financial regulator has banned all short selling of local stocks below the previous day’s closing price. The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) announced the move on Saturday, Bloomberg reported. It takes effect on 23 November.

Short selling is a bet that a share price will fall. The ban covers both margin short sales and sales of borrowed shares. Securities and futures firms that short stocks to hedge their business are exempt.

The FSC also raised the minimum margin for short sales to 150% from 130%. In addition, it stopped taking applications from brokers to list new put warrants, which also pay out when prices fall.

Industry observers note that it is the third round of short-selling curbs this month. On 9 November, the FSC cut the cap on intraday short sales of borrowed shares from 30% to 3% of average daily volume, Crowdfund Insider reported.

A second round on 19 November banned shorting below the previous close for stocks that fell at least 3.5% the day before, according to Focus Taiwan.

Industry observers note that neither round stopped the slide. The Taiex fell 6.2% on Friday and lost almost 18% over the week, its worst week since 1991, according to Bloomberg. Doubts about whether AI spending will pay off have hit tech shares across Asia.

Meanwhile, Taiwan’s NT$500bn ($15bn) National Financial Stabilization Fund remarked it has been buying shares since 6 November. The fund said worries about tighter US regulation of AI, returns on significant capital spending and margin-financing risks had triggered the sell-off.

Taiwan’s finance ministry mentioned the economy remains strong. It grew 14.4% in the third quarter, and October export orders rose 78% from a year earlier, Bloomberg reported.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts. If you’re shopping for AirPods, Apple sells three different models: AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods Max 2. Here’s how they compare.

AirPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions. Unlike their predecessors, both versions of AirPods 5 offer Active Noise Cancellation. They differ in the charging case, battery life, and volume control. The base model AirPods 5 ($129) come with a case that can only charge via USB-C.

According to recent reports, the case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My. You also get one extra hour of battery life. The higher-end model also adds on-stem volume control, so you can adjust the volume just by swiping up or down on one of the earbud stems.

Here’s a full comparison between both AirPods 5 models:.

The key thing about AirPods 5 is their open-ear design, unlike the in-ear design of the AirPods Pro 3 (more on those later). Even with that open-ear design, AirPods 5 offer incredible Active Noise Cancellation capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that if you are shopping for AirPods 5, I do recommend spending the extra $20 to get the higher-end model. The better charging case alone is worth the extra money. With Find My integration and a built-in speaker, you can track your AirPods and play a sound from the case if you lose them.

If the person you’re shopping for doesn’t like in-ear earbuds, AirPods 5 are an excellent choice.

For most people, though, AirPods Pro 3 are probably the better choice ….

AirPods Pro 3 are Apple’s most capable earbuds, even with the introduction of AirPods 5 this year. They offer an in-ear fit and come with five foam-infused silicone ear tip sizes. With that in-ear design, AirPods Pro 3 can offer up to 3x stronger noise cancellation than AirPods 5. In my testing, this difference is notable.

AirPods Pro 3 also offer several other features you won’t find on AirPods 5, including a heart rate sensor for workouts, plus Hearing Test, Hearing Aid, and Hearing Protection features.

I still think AirPods Pro 3 are one of the best products in Apple’s lineup today. I wear mine for multiple hours every single day and can’t imagine life without them. I love the in-ear fit, and the ANC still impresses me, whether I’m at home or somewhere like a coffee shop.

If you know the person you’re shopping for (whether it’s yourself or someone else) likes the in-ear earbud design, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option. This is especially true when AirPods Pro 3 are on sale, like they are right now at $179. The price difference between AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 is very small, and you’re getting a much better product.

Finally, we have AirPods Max. These are Apple’s only option for people who want AirPods in an over-ear headphone form factor. Last year, they were pretty hard to recommend since they’d gone five years without a real upgrade.

This year, however, Apple officially introduced AirPods Max 2, bringing modern features to Apple’s high-end headphones. This includes features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Personalized Volume, and more.

It has been revealed that airPods Max 2 are a far more compelling option than AirPods Max were at this time last year. They’re still pricey, but I love the aesthetics and find them very comfortable. There’s something about the premium aluminum design with an elegant Digital Crown that really stands out.

If you’re looking to splurge this holiday season, AirPods Max 2 are a great choice. For more realistic budgets, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option.

Are you planning to buy anyone AirPods this holiday season? Are they on your wishlist? Let us know down in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for a lot of commuters who want an electric scooter to get to and from work, you don’t need a tricked-out ride that costs over $1,000 and keeps up with the Porsches on the road.
  • I’ve recently been testing two scooters — the Apollo Dash and the Segway E3 Go — which are made for commuters, and can be purchased for less than $600.
  • The Apollo Dash has a top speed of 22 MPH, a max range of 25 miles, and has a 600W motor and 480Wh battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for a lot of commuters who want an electric scooter to get to and from work, you don’t need a tricked-out ride that costs over $1,000 and keeps up with the Porsches on the road. Something much more modest — and affordable will do the trick.

I’ve recently been testing two scooters — the Apollo Dash and the Segway E3 Go — which are made for commuters, and can be purchased for less than $600. I’ve found them to be fairly evenly matched, so to help you decide which is best for your needs, I’ve broken things down into a round-by-round comparison.

The Apollo Dash has a top speed of 22 MPH, a max range of 25 miles, and has a 600W motor and 480Wh battery.

The Segway E3 Go has a top speed of 20 MPH, a max range of 25 miles, a 400W motor, and front suspension.

The Apollo Dash is regularly priced at $699, but as of this writing, is on sale for $529 at Apollo.com; the Segway E3 Go is regularly $649, but for Black Friday, I've seen it on sale for $449.

Both of these scooters cut a pretty sleek profile. I personally like the cleaner lines of the Apollo as it transitions from the downtube to the deck; Segway’s folding mechanism, as well as its front suspension, makes things look a little busier.

According to recent reports, however, from a comfort standpoint, I liked the raked handlebars of the Segway over the Apollo, and the fact that the turn signal switch is located by your left thumb. By comparison, the Dash requires you to use your right thumb to activate the right turn signal, which means you have to take your thumb off the throttle.

Recent findings suggest that the display is one area where Segway and Apollo really differ; the E3 Go has a more traditional color LCD screen that indicates your speed and battery life. The Dash, on the other hand, uses a grid of white LEDs, which also shows your speed and battery life in a more basic way. However, The Apollo Dash also has a quad lock mount just below, so if you have a compatible phone case, you can use your phone as a digital dashboard.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I like the folding mechanism on both scooters; you can collapse them in mere seconds, but I'm giving the advantage here to Segway. You can simply press on a flap with your foot, so you don't have to lean down.

It has been revealed that apollo’s scooter is slightly lighter than Segway’s — 43 pounds as opposed to 46.7 pounds. You’re going to get a workout either way.

Recent findings suggest that one of my biggest concerns as a rider is being seen by other drivers. The Apollo’s large light bar, which extends the length of the downtube, makes you far more noticeable at night. In addition, you can adjust the angle of its headlight. By comparison, the Segway’s headlight is fixed, and it has no other lights in the front.

Both scooters have turn signals in the handlebars; however, only Apollo lets you adjust how long they remain on; from within the app, you can set a period from seven seconds or until you deactivate it.

I still wish both had turn signals in the rear of the scooter too, like the Segway Max G3 Plus or the Apollo City.

According to recent reports, on my steep hill test (which has a max grade of 10%), the Segway slowed down to 4 MPH on the steepest section; I had to do a little wiggling of the handlebars to keep it balanced. By comparison, the Apollo managed to get up the same hill at 8 MPH — not exactly a speed record, but it was twice as fast as the Segway.

On a hill with a less steep grade of 5.7%, both scooters performed about the same, slowing to around 12 MPH.

Recent findings suggest that the raked handlebars, front suspension, and larger tires of the Segway E3 Go really made a difference, especially at speed. The scooter felt more stable when I was cruising at 20+ MPH, and was much less jarring than the suspension-less Apollo when I went over bumps and potholes.

Both the Apollo and Segway are rated for a max distance of 25 miles, but that’s assuming ideal conditions, and if you poke along at around 9 MPH on a flat road. With both scooters at full charge, Segway estimated that it had 11.2 miles of range, compared to 17 for the Apollo when both were set to their max performance levels. If you want to eke out a bit more range, both scooters offer regenerative braking.

Sources indicate that I took them one at a time on an identical 5.5-mile loop around my town, going up and down the same hills. After a 5.5-mile ride, the Apollo had 55% battery left, while Segway’s had just 32%.

Now, range will vary greatly from one rider to another, but I suspect that the more powerful motor in the Apollo scooter enabled it to use power more efficiently during my test.

Sources indicate that both Segway’s and Apollo’s apps let you customize how the scooter performs, to a certain extent. For example, with each, you can specify the max speed for each performance setting, so if you don’t want to zoom along at 20 MPH in Sport mode, you don’t have to.

However, Apollo’s app offers a bit more customization. You can, for instance, set the amount of time that the turn signals remain on, and also fine-tune the throttle response, if you want to get off to a faster start.

Industry observers note that after testing both the Apollo Dash and the Segway E3 Go, neither really pulls away from the other to make this a decisive victory. Still, over these seven rounds, the Apollo Dash takes this matchup, winning four rounds to the Segway E3 Go’s three.

I liked the design of the Segway’s handlebars and controls, and it felt more comfortable and stable while riding. And, at the time of this writing, it was $80 cheaper. However, the Apollo Dash proved more capable when scooting up hills, its lighting makes it far more visible, and it had a better range in my testing.

If you don't have hills to climb, then the Segway would be the better pick, but if you're facing some inclines, then I would lean towards the Apollo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when I think about Adam Driver as an actor, two words come to mind: stoic and intense. I see a disciplined actor with no social media presence who lets his work speak for itself.

It has been revealed that part of that discipline comes from his military background, while the rest stems from his time at Juilliard. Driver would have loved to come up in the 1960s and 1970s, as he feels cut from the same cloth as Robert De Niro and Al Pacino.

Currently, Driver stars in “Paper Tiger,” James Gray’s New York City crime drama about two brothers whose business dealings become entangled with the Russian mob. Driver has received rave reviews for his performance, with some critics calling it the actor’s best work. In honor of “Paper Tiger,” here are Driver's five best movies.

Sources indicate that the irony of Driver’s career is that despite being known for his intensity, he’s extremely funny. Driver’s breakout role came as Adam Sackler in the HBO comedy “Girls.” Since this list concerns movies, I’ll select another project from that era: “What If,” or in some territories, “The F Word.” (“What If” is a better title, for what it’s worth.) One night, Wallace (Daniel Radcliffe) and Chantry (Zoe Kazan) meet and hit it off. Although Chantry has a boyfriend, Wallace elects to be her friend because he’s in love with her.

Sources indicate that wallace and Chantry seem perfect for each other, but bad timing and unfortunate circumstances keep them apart. Driver plays Allan, Wallace’s best friend. Allan is a boisterous friend who encourages Wallace to tell Chantry how he feels. “What If” is a charming rom-com with a hilarious performance from Driver, who deserves recognition for his line delivery in the “greatest moment of my life” speech.

Like many “Star Wars” fans, I have problems with the sequel trilogy. My biggest gripe is with “The Rise of Skywalker,” especially the entire Palpatine debacle. It’s difficult to tell the story of Driver’s career without a “Star Wars” movie, so I’ll go with “The Force Awakens,” the highly entertaining popcorn blockbuster that kicked off Lucasfilm’s Disney era. Thirty years after the events of “Return of the Jedi,” the galaxy faces a newly introduced Imperial threat: the First Order.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Resistance, led by General Leia Organa (Carrie Fisher), recruits a new set of rebels, including Poe Dameron (Oscar Isaac), Finn (John Boyega), and Rey (Daisy Ridley). Driver plays Kylo Ren, a ruthless warrior in the First Order out to find the location of Luke Skywalker. Driver’s intensity translates seamlessly to a villainous role. Kylo is Gen Z’s version of Darth Vader. Driver plays Ren as a brooding, sad boy with daddy issues. It’s a subversion of masculinity and an interesting addition to the “Star Wars” lineup of iconic villains.

According to recent reports, spike Lee mentioned it best. While speaking with BBC Radio 1 for “BlacKkKlansman,” Lee described Driver as a “beast.” Lee went on to praise Driver’s range as an actor. No arguments here, Mr. Lee. In “BlacKkKlansman,” John David Washington stars as Ron Stallworth, the first Black detective in the Colorado Springs Police Department.

Recent findings suggest that looking to infiltrate the local Ku Klux Klan, Ron poses as a white supremacist over the phone. The Klan buys it and wants to meet Ron. Since he’s Black, Ron recruits his white Jewish co-worker, Flip Zimmerman (Driver), to pose as him. The ruse works, and the duo infiltrates the Ku Klux Klan to thwart its nefarious aims. “BlacKkKlansman” is a witty and sharp critique of racism and extremist political movements.

It has been revealed that it’s also a film that eerily resembles events from the current day, which is scary in itself. Driver’s grounded presence is the perfect counterbalance to Washington’s excessive charisma. Driver earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor, the first of his career.

I enjoy Driver as a heel. He knows how to get under my skin as a villain. He did it in “Star Wars,” and he arguably did it better in “The Last Duel.” Ridley Scott’s period piece is based on the last trial by combat in medieval France. The movie is split into three parts, detailing the viewpoints of Jean de Carrouges (Matt Damon), Jacques le Gris (Driver), and Marguerite de Carrouges (Jodie Comer).

In a recent development, marguerite accuses Jacques of rape while Jean is out of town. With no physical evidence, it becomes Marguerite’s word versus Jacques’s, with the latter vehemently denying the accusation. Believing he must defend his family's honor, Jean requests a duel to the death, which Jacques accepts.

Recent findings suggest that don’t let the box office failures turn you away from this excellent drama and Scott’s best movie this decade. It’s a shockingly violent movie, but also one that rewards patience. It’s not good vs. bad. Instead, it’s about morally complex characters, making for a far more interesting dilemma.

If I were having trouble in a relationship, “Marriage Story” might be at the bottom of the pile of films to watch. Noah Baumbach’s drama about a couple going through a divorce features some of the meanest, rawest, and most emotional scenes I’ve ever seen. At times, it punches you in the heart and makes you question everything you knew about love. At the center of the movie are Charlie (Driver) and Nicole Barber (Scarlett Johansson), a married couple.

Charlie, a theater director, and Nicole, an actress, agree to a divorce. Charlie remains in Fresh York, while Nicole heads to Los Angeles with their son, Henry (Azhy Robertson). The couple begins divorce proceedings cordially, but when lawyers get involved, it becomes cutthroat. Some of these scenes between Charlie and Nicole, especially the climactic argument, are like watching a car crash — you can’t look away. It’s an acting tour de force for Driver and Johansson, who earned their respective Oscar nominations.

According to recent reports, most of what Siri documents, I’ll never need to reference and it gets deleted automatically. But for those times I have trouble remembering a key piece of information, I’ve found Siri Recap a very convenient addition.

Apple Watch Series 12 offers largely the same battery life as Series 11, though it will last 25% longer for outdoor workouts.

Industry observers note that I wear my Apple Watch to bed and generally try to top it off promptly in the evening, but I’m not always great at giving it much time on the charger. With faster charging support on Series 12, my poor planning isn’t a problem.

In the fiscal year ended July 3, 2026, free cash flow was nearly $11.5 billion. This cash generation provides the business with the flexibility to reinvest in its flash storage research and development.

According to recent reports, micron Technology faces significant risks from the inherent cyclicality of the memory market, where selling prices can fluctuate wildly. The company is also highly dependent on a small group of large data center customers. Intense competition from firms like Samsung and SK hynix (SKHY -13.11%) keeps pressure on innovation and pricing. Furthermore, trade restrictions involving China, as well as the CAC's restrictions on purchasing its products, could disrupt its global operations or limit its market access.

Sources indicate that sandisk relies heavily on strategic joint ventures, specifically with Flash Ventures and Kioxia, which can limit its ability to make independent operational decisions. The company also faces intense competition, which can lead to lower average selling prices for flash memory. Forecasting the specific needs of AI infrastructure remains difficult, creating a risk of supply imbalances. Additionally, its recent separation from Western Digital (WDC -12.02%) introduces ongoing regulatory and compliance complexities.

Sandisk carries a lower multiple relative to future earnings estimates, while Micron looks more attractive based on its current relationship with trailing sales.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The Forward P/E uses future earnings estimates to gauge value, while the P/S ratio measures market cap against sales over the past twelve months.

Both stocks need the same thing to go right: AI data center spending has to keep growing. Last week's AI sell-off, which dragged chip stocks lower and gave the S&P 500 its worst week in more than a year and a half, showed how promptly investors can doubt that. It hit Micron and Sandisk alike, so the drop tells you little about which business is better built.What separates them is how each handles a slowdown. Micron runs its own fabs, sells across DRAM, HBM and NAND, and holds far more cash than debt, so it can keep investing through a rough patch. Sandisk runs leaner and spends little on capital, but it sells only NAND and relies on one joint venture partner for its wafers.For a long-term investor, that points to Micron. Last week lowered the price you pay, but it didn't make memory any less cyclical, and drops like this can run further. Build a position in stages rather than all at once, and size it so another leg down wouldn't force you to sell. If your timeline is 2027 and beyond, the real test is whether you can hold through the swings, not whether you catch the bottom.

Tech Report: I drove the Audi Q3 and Mini Countryman for a week — here’s the sub-$52K crossover I’d buy with my own money

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that each of them has a distinct take on the "sensibly priced" formula, delivering upscale tech, all-wheel drive, and genuine everyday utility without drifting into absurd price territory.
  • In a recent development, with an as-tested price of $44,250, it undercuts the $51,790 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro by a wide margin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when I think about luxury vehicles, the first things that instantly come to mind are $60,000+ price tags. Thankfully, entry-level luxury crossovers exist, and they’re some of the smartest buys on the market. For my next comparison, I’m pitting the Mini Countryman and Audi Q3 against each other in a head-to-head matchup to see which compact crossover is worth buying.

It has been revealed that each of them has a distinct take on the "sensibly priced" formula, delivering upscale tech, all-wheel drive, and genuine everyday utility without drifting into absurd price territory. It’s actually been years since I last tested a Mini — the electric Countryman EV — so you can imagine how eager I was to get back into the gas-powered 2027 Mini Countryman S All4.

In a recent development, with an as-tested price of $44,250, it undercuts the $51,790 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro by a wide margin. I will say, however, that you can’t dismiss the Q3 just yet, because after a week’s worth of driving, it too impressed me on plenty of occasions.

2.0L TFSI turbocharged I4 Engine.

2.0-Liter MINI TwinPower Turbo Inline 4-Cylinder Engine.

22 mpg city / 29 mpg highway / 25 mpg combined.

24 mpg city / 32 mpg highway / 27 mpg combined.

Frankly, this one’s tough because these compact crossovers cater to completely different tastes, so personal preference heavily influences the decision.

The 2026 Audi Q3 leans heavily into conventional luxury aesthetics, dressed in Malpelo Blue Metallic with the Black Optic package — which shimmers in the light. Alongside the sharp LED headlights up front and OLED taillights in the back, the package makes it look sleek and unmistakably upscale.

By contrast, the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 embraces a sportier edge and distinctive British flair. It’s undeniably boxier and more upright, yet it’s loaded with personality — I especially love its Slate Blue Metallic paint job with a contrasting black roof and stripes. Even its LED lighting features customizable light signatures to match its charming looks.

Ultimately, it comes down to whether you prefer understated German luxury or retro-modern charm — making this category an easy tie.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Best short distance fuel economy.

Best long distance fuel economy.

Looking at their spec sheets, it’s quite clear that the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 holds a slight advantage in terms of fuel economy with an EPA-estimated 27 mpg combined (24 city / 32 highway), compared to the 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro’s 25 mpg combined rating (22 city / 29 highway).

In my real-world testing, however, that gap turned into a surprisingly wide canyon. Over 313.6 miles of mixed driving in the Countryman, I averaged an impressive 31.1 mpg overall — easily exceeding its EPA estimate. Better yet, it hit 30.5 mpg on my best short-distance trip and soared to 36.1 mpg on a longer highway stretch.

In contrast, the Audi Q3 struggled to match its window sticker across 243.5 miles of testing, averaging just 23.2 mpg overall. Even on my best long-distance (26.5 mpg) run, it never came close to its 29 mpg highway rating.

If keeping fuel costs low is a top priority, the Mini is the clear standout here, saving you noticeably more at the pump in the long run.

It has been revealed that most compact crossovers prioritize fuel economy and put driving dynamics in the back seat, but not these two. Better yet, I love how both prove you don’t need a massive engine to have fun behind the wheel.

The 2027 Mini Countryman S All4 is my favorite of the two by a narrow margin, packing a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four engine that puts out 241 horsepower and 295 lb-ft of torque. The Audi similarly has impressive muscle under the hood: a 2.0-liter TFSI four-cylinder that delivers 255 horsepower and 273 lb-ft of torque.

It has been revealed that what I will say after being behind the wheel of both is that they’re noticeably zippy off the line, with speedy acceleration that makes it effortless to overtake at cruising speed. While the Q3’s powertrain actually surprised me with a smooth delivery that almost makes it feel more like an EV, it doesn’t beat the Countryman when the road starts to curve. The Mini's lower, wider stance keeps it feeling noticeably more planted through corners, preserving that signature go-kart agility it’s known for.

It has been revealed that despite their smaller footprints, these compact crossovers still offer plenty of room to make lengthy road trips a breeze. However, the 2027 Mini Countryman S All4 holds a slight advantage. That’s because it offers 40.4 inches of front legroom and 37 inches in the rear, which beats the 2026 Audi Q3’s 40 inches up front and 36.1 inches in the back. Additionally, they deliver nearly identical trunk space around 25 cubic feet, easily accommodating my electric scooter.

Inside, they take very different approaches to cabin materials. The Audi leans into traditional luxury with genuine leather seating surfaces, wood inlays, and solid soundproofing that keeps road noise at a minimum. Obviously, the higher price of the Q3 is justified by its more luxurious aesthetics.

Mini takes a totally different approach that gives it a charming style that feels genuinely original. It trades classic leather for Vescin leather-free upholstery and knitted textile surfaces on the dash and doors — which I have to say looked funky and stylish at first glance, but they eventually grew on me.

Industry observers note that sure, the Audi comes up a smidge short on rear legroom, but the Q3 just feels noticeably more plush over long stretches. And when I factor in Audi’s smoother, more intuitive adaptive cruise assist on highways, the Q3 edges ahead as the more relaxing cruiser.

According to recent reports, audi needs to prove it’s worth spending about $7,500 more over its rival. But does it?

While the 2026 Audi Q3 doesn’t skimp on luxury amenities, it simply makes you pay noticeably more for them. Even so, I appreciate its crisp 360-degree camera coverage, head-up display that projects driving details onto the windshield to lessen distractions, and seamless Park Assist Plus for automatic parking. Inside, its panoramic sunroof and vibrant LED ambient lighting create a more upscale look at night — while its large blind-spot warning lights mounted right on the side mirrors are impossible to miss in heavy traffic or in the daytime.

In a recent development, however, you’re still getting better value for the money out of the Mini Countryman S ALL4. For starters, its circular 9.4-inch OLED touchscreen display is a sight to behold and runs a far more intuitive interface. Although it ditches the traditional driver’s cluster entirely, the flip-up head-up display keeps distractions at a minimum. I’m also significant on sound, and the punchy Harman Kardon surround sound system easily outclasses the Audi's Sonos setup.

Industry observers note that not only does it offer full 360-degree camera coverage, but it also includes a clever Backup Assistant that takes over the wheel and automatically retraces the path I took to get into the spot. And finally, I really love the adaptive LED headlights with customizable light signatures and cornering lights.

When I weigh this robust feature set against that $7,540 price gap, the Mini delivers far more bang for your buck.

Let me finish by saying that I’d gladly buy either compact crossover in a heartbeat with my own money. That remarked, the 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro does come up short once the tallies are counted.

If you prioritize traditional luxury materials, a quieter cabin, and a smoother adaptive cruise control system for long highway commutes, it remains an immensely likable daily driver that costs less than the average luxury vehicle. Honestly, despite losing this head-to-head matchup, I would still gladly buy the Audi Q3 — it’s just that the Mini Countryman gives you more for less.

Industry observers note that the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 emerges as the clear winner, and it’s the one I’d ultimately pick. Between its punchy driving dynamics, standout real-world fuel economy, sharper OLED infotainment system, and $7,540 price advantage in this comparison, it simply delivers too much personality and value to ignore.

Among iOS 27’s many latest features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces substantial AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting latest features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the revision also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

Here’s how it works, per Apple:.

According to recent reports, after iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

Industry observers note that to move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

It has been revealed that most users will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

Sources indicate that I feel like I’m exactly who this feature was made for. After years of running dual SIM, I now have a personal line on my Duo and work line on an 18 Pro. Going out with friends, family, etc, I’d love to bring one phone again while bringing both numbers with me, but keeping work system access to a specific, separate device. Only current problem is waiting for Verizon to activate the feature and then see if it actually works well.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”.

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple plans to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

How to clear slippery moss and green algae from patio pavers — without blasting out the sand

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that damp, shady weather turns even the best-kept patio into a slippery green mess, and reaching for a pressure washer is not always the smartest fix.
  • According to recent reports, fortunately, you do not need heavy machinery to get your patio looking clean and safe underfoot again.
  • While a power washer strips surface grime in minutes, it only removes the visible top layer of moss and algae, leaving microscopic spores behind in the pores of the stone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that damp, shady weather turns even the best-kept patio into a slippery green mess, and reaching for a pressure washer is not always the smartest fix. High-pressure jets can blast jointing sand straight out from between your pavers, pit soft natural stone, and leave behind micro-scratches where moss and algae grow back even faster.

According to recent reports, fortunately, you do not need heavy machinery to get your patio looking clean and safe underfoot again. A stiff broom, a watering can, and a few simple household staples or outdoor treatments are all it takes to lift stubborn green growth without damaging your stonework.

While a power washer strips surface grime in minutes, it only removes the visible top layer of moss and algae, leaving microscopic spores behind in the pores of the stone. Worse still, blasting delicate limestone, sandstone, or older mortar joints with high-pressure water erodes the surface and loosens the pavers themselves.

It has been revealed that gentle cleaning methods work differently. Instead of relying on brute force, they break down the organic growth at the root so you can brush or rinse it away cleanly, keeping both your stone surface and the sand between your pavers intact.

Before applying any cleaner, move patio furniture out of the way, sweep away loose leaves with a stiff broom (avoid metal rakes, which can scratch pavers), and lightly water any nearby lawn or flowerbeds so plants do not absorb soapy or acidic runoff.

Once prepped, choose the method that best suits your patio material:.

If you have delicate natural stone like limestone or sandstone, or simply want the gentlest fix, start with a bucket of warm water and a few generous squeezes of dish soap.

Recent findings suggest that pour the sudsy mixture over the pavers, let it sit for 15 minutes to loosen the grime, and scrub diagonally across the joints with a stiff outdoor brush so you do not dislodge the sand. Rinse thoroughly with a garden hose.

For heavier green buildup on concrete or brick pavers, wet the patio down first, scatter washing soda crystals (sodium carbonate) across the affected areas, and add a small drizzle of dish soap.

Work the paste into the pavers with a stiff brush, then leave it to sit for 24 to 48 hours before hosing it away. Always wear gloves when handling soda crystals, and keep pets off the patio until it is rinsed clean.

Skip this method on natural stone: because vinegar is acidic, it can etch and discolor limestone, sandstone, or travertine.

Mix equal parts white vinegar and water in a watering can or garden sprayer, saturate the mossy patches, and leave the solution to soak for 20 to 30 minutes before scrubbing with a stiff brush and rinsing well.

In a recent development, if you are tackling a large patio or stubborn black-spot lichen, an oxygen- or enzyme-based outdoor paver cleaner saves hours of scrubbing. Apply the solution with a watering can on a dry day, leave it to break down the spores over a few days, and let the next rainfall wash the dead growth away naturally.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Micah Zimmerman – Nov 22, 2026 at 1:45PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Walmart ›.

In a recent development, walmart (WMT +1.51%) had a good morning on Thursday, Nov. 19. Sales and profit topped Wall Street's estimates, and the tech giant raised its full-year forecast. Then the stock fell about 2% in early trading anyway.

I've learned to love earnings days like this. A dip on good news is often the cheapest way into a company that has raised its dividend for 53 straight years. This move of 50 consecutive dividend raises places Walmart in the coveted Dividend King category. These are companies that have raised their payouts for 50 years or more.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

CEO John Furner summed up the quarter in one line: "The strength of our omnichannel model gives us room to do even more.".

What he means is that Walmart's stores are no longer just places you walk into to make a purchase. They have become launchpads for online orders, and more than a third of the orders filled from stores reached shoppers in under three hours. That speed is winning new kinds of customers, too, as Walmart stated its share gains were led by upper-income households.

CFO John David Rainey said the quarter also brought Walmart's biggest market share gains in food in three years. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses," he told CNBC.

It has been revealed that the part I find most exciting doesn't involve a shopping cart at all. Walmart's U.S. advertising business grew 37%, its membership fee revenue rose 17% worldwide, and sales on its online marketplace, where outside sellers pay to reach Walmart's shoppers, jumped 49%.

Industry observers note that brands pay to show up where millions of people shop, and members pay a yearly fee whether they buy a TV or a gallon of milk. That's how Walmart can keep cutting prices and still grow profit, and it's what makes the dividend feel so durable to me.

Then there's Sparky, Walmart's AI shopping assistant. Its U.S. usage has more than doubled from a year ago, and Furner noted shoppers who use it build baskets about 40% bigger on average. Shopping may increasingly start with a question typed into an app instead of a walk down an aisle, and Walmart wants to be the one answering it.

Recent findings suggest that the newest piece is a $120-a-year bundle of Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus. Furner told CNBC it has brought about 2 million new people into Sam's Club since it released in late October, and Rainey said bundle members are "spending appreciably more." There's a catch, though: Walmart expects the bundle to weigh on Sam's Club profit growth until late 2027.

My reason is a practical one. Walmart's next dividend goes to shareholders of record on Dec. 11, so you need to own shares by the ex-dividend date. Walmart has also repurchased $7.8 billion of its own stock so far this fiscal year, so the dividend isn't the only way it returns cash. The holiday season is arriving, too, and Rainey mentioned he's "optimistic" about holiday spending, adding that the fourth quarter is "off to a pretty good start.".

Here's what gives me pause. Diesel prices are climbing. "The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into the cost of goods," Furner told CNBC, adding that "we'll keep prices as low as we can.".

U.S. same-store sales growth also slowed to 2.9%, from 4.5% a year ago. Rainey stated Walmart is keeping "flexibility" in its forecast, and the stock already trades at about 46 times earnings with a dividend yield under 1%. That's a rich P/E ratio for a store, and the yield won't make anyone rich quickly.

According to recent reports, so why never sell the stock? Walmart has turned its stores into delivery hubs, its shoppers into an ad audience, and its customers into paying members. Each of those makes the others stronger, and that's the kind of economic moat that tends to widen with age.

The 53-year streak is the result of a business that keeps finding newly introduced ways to earn its customers' trust, and today's report showed it's still doing exactly that.

#119697. Perplexity and Intelligence
