10 stocks we like better than Broadcom ›.

According to recent reports, broadcom (AVGO -12.19%) has become one of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure boom. Demand for its custom AI chips and networking gear is surging as tech giants pour billions of dollars into data centers. Last quarter, its AI semiconductor revenue rocketed 221% to $16.7 billion, and management expects that business to double in fiscal 2027 and again in fiscal 2028.

Industry observers note that the stock, however, already prices in a lot of that success. While it currently trades about 30% below its 52-week high, it's still up nearly 250% over the past three years. Here's a look at what a $1,000 investment in Broadcom could be worth by 2035.

Broadcom's fiscal 2026 third quarter was its best yet. Total revenue rose 86% to $29.6 billion, and AI semiconductor revenue climbed 221% to $16.7 billion. For the fourth quarter, the organization guided to $21.7 billion in AI revenue, up 236%. Management has also laid out a path to roughly $58 billion of AI semiconductor revenue in fiscal 2026, $115 billion in fiscal 2027, and $230 billion in fiscal 2028. Custom accelerators for customers such as Anthropic and OpenAI drive that growth, along with the Ethernet switching and optical connections that link those chips together.

According to recent reports, broadcom isn't just an AI chip story. Its infrastructure software business, anchored by VMware, recorded nearly $8.8 billion in revenue last quarter, up 29%. That high-margin business generates growing recurring revenue for the tech giant.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Investor expectations are as major as the AI opportunity. So are the risks. Broadcom depends on a small group of AI infrastructure customers, so a spending pullback by even one could hurt. AI spending could also cool once the current build-out peaks, and some customers may struggle to finance or monetize their data centers. Worries about AI financing and customer concentration have already driven a sell-off in chip stocks.

Margins are another watch item. As lower-margin custom accelerators account for a larger share of sales, margins could shrink. Competition from rivals and in-house chip designs also adds margin risk.

The question isn't whether AI infrastructure spending will grow over time. It's whether Broadcom can deliver the profits that investors already assume.

Industry observers note that broadcom recently traded around $325 per share. Analysts expect about $19.39 in adjusted earnings per share (EPS) for fiscal 2027, which puts the stock at roughly 17 times that estimate. Wall Street is bullish: none of the 50 analysts covering the manufacturer rate it a sell, and the average price target is over $525 a share. That estimate already assumes more than 60% upside from the recent price.

To cover all the bases, I modeled three scenarios to 2035:.

Here's what a $1,000 investment in Broadcom stock would be worth in 2035 under those scenarios:.

It has been revealed that all three scenarios include estimated cash dividends, without reinvestment, and assume a purchase at today's price. The base case is conservative next to management's own goal: CEO Hock Tan has said Broadcom is on target to exceed $30 of EPS in fiscal 2028, while my base case implies about $21 that year. However, even in a conservative base case, Broadcom could deliver a nearly 150% return. Meanwhile, the bull case is even stronger.

According to recent reports, broadcom has a compelling opportunity in custom AI chips and networking, and its software business adds another source of profitable growth. Under my base case, a $1,000 investment in the semiconductor stock could grow to about $2,500 by 2035, a nearly 11% annualized total return. That's an attractive return, and it doesn't require Broadcom to sustain its extraordinary near-term growth indefinitely. While the outcome depends on the manufacturer meeting very ambitious earnings expectations, Broadcom looks like a compelling AI stock to buy right now.

I tested the iPhone 18 Pro Max vs Xiaomi 18 Pro Max in a 11-round camera shootout — here is the winner

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the iPhone 18 Pro Max isn't the only 18 Pro Max to be released this year, now that Xiaomi has just revealed the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max flagships.
  • The iPhone 18 Pro Max is one of the best camera phones, sporting a trio of 48MP camera lenses: one main, with variable aperture, an ultrawide angle, and a telephoto lens with 4x optical zoom.
  • You'd think that the higher resolution camera would produce the best photos, right?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the iPhone 18 Pro Max isn't the only 18 Pro Max to be released this year, now that Xiaomi has just revealed the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max flagships. The two phones share more than just a name, though, and it seems Xiaomi has adopted a very Apple-looking camera bump on the back of its phones. But considering the camera specs are totally different, I started wondering what the actual quality differences were.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is one of the best camera phones, sporting a trio of 48MP camera lenses: one main, with variable aperture, an ultrawide angle, and a telephoto lens with 4x optical zoom. The zooming camera offers up to 16x "optical quality" and has a maximum magnification of 40x. The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, on the other hand, has a 200MP main lens, a 50MP ultrawide and a 200MP telephoto with 3.2x optical zoom.

You'd think that the higher resolution camera would produce the best photos, right? Well we've seen time and again that resolution doesn't always equal quality, especially now that camera phones rely on software just as much as they do hardware. That's why phones like the iPhone 18 Pro Max perform so well in our photo shootouts.

It has been revealed that but obviously the only way to find out for sure is to actually take some photos and compare the results from each phone. So, out of iPhone 18 Pro Max and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which 18 Pro Max actually has the best cameras?

The latest and best iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes with a fresh variable aperture camera, a larger battery, incredible performance from the A20 Pro chipset and all those other things that make the iPhone worth owning.

While not officially available in the U.S., the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max has a lot of great features. They include a rear-mounted display, 200MP main and telephoto camera lenses, a 6.98-inch display with Privacy Display and an enormous 7,050 mAh battery.

The main camera shot is quite different on both phones. The Xiaomi certainly excels in taking a brighter photo, but the result means that the lighter areas look considerably more washed out compared to the iPhone. The overall quality isn't as good either, since the iPhone can pick up more detail in the surroundings, such as my dogs' fur and the gravel on the path. In contrast, the Xiaomi tends to blur those finer details together, especially in the background.

Shooting indoors, things are a little more balanced, but it's clear that the Xiaomi's camera isn't quite as focused as the iPhone's, and most of the Lego set is blurry in comparison to Apple's camera. However the coloring and detail seem to be much closer than they were with the outdoor shot.

The Xiaomi camera's habit of brightening up the image seems to work in its favor on the ultrawide angle lens, with the iPhone adopting a more washed out and drab-looking color temperature. There are reasons for that, and it all comes down to Apple's automatic white balance being somewhat anti-Fall.

However, coloring aside, the detail on the iPhone-captured shot just isn't there. You can even see it in the grass if you look closely, with all the stalks looking pixelated and blurred, compared to the much sharper detail captured by the Xiaomi.

In a recent development, when it comes to color, the Xiaomi does edge the top spot with slightly more vivid coloring of these berries, in part thanks to the slightly brighter images. The iPhone hasn't washed out the coloring in this instance, and manages to offer a nice bright image with solid contrast between the different colors.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's front camera sports a 50MP sensor, compared to the 18MP one on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but how much of a difference does it make? As was the case with the rear cameras, the photo is a lot brighter, which really highlights the fact that the sun is shining directly onto my face. Meanwhile the iPhone's shot is a little darker, but the tones seem more true to life and don't make it look like this is my first time outside in several months.

Sources indicate that the quality is good on both, even going so far as to pick up the reflection of my other dog in my sunglasses. However, zooming in indicates how much of a difference high resolution can make. Xiaomi's rendition of my reflected dog is clear and almost perfect, while the iPhone's is pixelated and grainy. Then again, the rest of the photo is fine, and zooming right in isn't something a lot of folks will be doing.

Xiaomi's Portrait mode is, honestly, incredibly disappointing. The bokeh effect is barely noticeable, and it doesn't really emphasize myself in the same way that the iPhone does. The IPhone 18 Pro Max ramped up that effect to the point where the background isn't that visible, and it makes me pop out a little more. The quality of the photo isn't quite as good, but with the extra bokeh and the return more accurate coloring, it's the clear winner.

Recent findings suggest that zooming into 4x magnification and things are fairly even. The iPhone's coloring is a little more drab than Xiaomi's, but the overall quality of the zoomed-in shot is basically the same, to the point where it's more about personal preference than anything else.

It has been revealed that jumping up to 8x magnification and you can see how Apple's "optical quality" feature really shines. The shot of my dog at this magnification is much more clear than that of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which noticeably merges the finer details of my dog's fur. The contrasting colors on the Xiaomi's telephoto is more noticeable than the iPhone's, but the loss of quality really lets the team down.

If you increase the magnification to 40x, there's absolutely no question about which camera is better. It's Xiaomi's, simply because the phone produced a clear and crisp shot that the iPhone just can't compete with. I assume some AI upscaling was involved, as is the case with so many other phones, and it's something that Apple consistently fails at. Maybe that's something Apple can include on the iPhone 20.

According to recent reports, going right in with the Macro mode, and the iPhone takes the crown once again. As with before, the picture isn't as bright as Xiaomi's shot, but that doesn't actually matter in this case. The iPhone managed to produce a much crisper photo, with bright colors and details that Xiaomi's camera didn't quite match.

Low light performance can make or break a camera phone, and I'm honestly a little torn over which camera is better in this situation. The iPhone 18 Pro Max produced a shot that is brighter and captured more detail, but it also appears somewhat overexposed in the process.

Recent findings suggest that the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max managed to capture less detail on the church and its surroundings, despite the higher resolution camera, but produced a shot that looks slightly nicer — so long as you don't zoom in too much. And, honestly, I can't tell you which one I like better.

Overall, the iPhone 18 Pro Max managed to beat out the Xiaomi in more categories, though, the two phones drew in several rounds. That highlights that Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's camera is no slouch, but not enough to beat the iPhone's camera in those core categories. The quality of the 8x zoom in particular was especially disappointing, since a 200MP lens should have the resolution to be able to cut down a high-quality image to simulate extra magnification — just like Apple does.

Given the choice, and purely based on camera performance, I'd pick the iPhone 18 Pro Max over the Xiaomi. Still the iPhone 18 Pro Max didn't dominate, and the Xiaomi camera certainly manages to produce some great shots. The fact they tied in four different categories just goes to show that these two phones are both very capable camera phones.

But Xiaomi obviously needs to work on fixing its shortcomings, including capturing more detail in low light, improving the bokeh effect and all those other things that could make the camera even better.

10 stocks we like better than Lululemon Athletica Inc. ›.

Recent findings suggest that choosing between a premium apparel leader and a global fast-food titan requires weighing growth potential against steady income. Is lululemon athletica (LULU -2.76%) or McDonald's (MCD +0.33%) the better pick for 2027?

Lululemon athletica focuses on high-end technical gear for active lifestyles, leveraging deep brand loyalty to maintain premium pricing. McDonald's operates a massive real estate and franchising empire, providing consistent cash flow through essential dining. Both companies are titans of the consumer landscape, but they offer vastly different paths for retail investors.

It has been revealed that lululemon athletica sells footwear and accessories alongside its signature yoga and running gear to a loyal customer base. It reaches these guests through more than 800 manufacturer-operated stores and a robust e-commerce platform that drives significant engagement. These physical locations often serve as community hubs that offer fitness events to build brand equity and reach more consumers in the apparel stocks category.

In a recent development, in the 12 months ended Aug. 2, 2026, revenue reached nearly $11.1 billion, representing an increase of approximately 1.7% from the prior twelve-month period. Net income for this timeframe was close to $1.4 billion. This growth rate represents a normalization after the rapid expansion seen in previous years as the company focuses on international markets and men's apparel.

Industry observers note that as of its February 2026 balance sheet, the company maintained a healthy debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 0.4x. The current ratio, which measures short-term assets against liabilities, was approximately 2.3x. In the fiscal year ended Feb. 1, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $921.7 million, which is the cash left over after paying for operations and capital investments.

According to recent reports, mcDonald's operates as a global leader in the restaurant industry with a network of over 45,000 locations. Its highly successful franchise model allows the tech giant to collect consistent royalties and rent while shifting most operating costs to independent owners. It also leverages delivery partnerships with platforms like Uber to ensure its products remain accessible to a broad consumer base in over 100 countries.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $27.8 billion, representing growth of close to 5.8% compared to the prior twelve-month period. Net income during this same timeframe was nearly $9.0 billion. These strong figures highlight the resilience of a business that can effectively raise prices to manage inflationary pressures while maintaining high transaction volumes.

Industry observers note that as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly -30.6x, indicating that total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term debts, was approximately 1.0x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was close to $7.2 billion, providing ample capital for dividends and share repurchases.

lululemon athletica faces intense competition from established athletic brands and potential supply chain disruptions due to its manufacturing concentration in Asia. The firm must also manage the risks of a leadership transition following the departure of its CEO. Brand reputation remains a key vulnerability, as negative publicity or product defects could impact consumer loyalty in the premium segment.

It has been revealed that mcDonald's depends on the financial success of its franchisees and faces stiff competition in the global informal dining market. Operational risks include food safety concerns and commodity price volatility that can impact restaurant profitability. The tech giant also must invest heavily to protect its digital systems against data security and cybersecurity threats that target its ordering platforms.

Lululemon athletica looks considerably cheaper than McDonald's when comparing their Forward P/E and P/S ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

I'd go with McDonald's. It has built one of the world's best-known restaurant brands, and its franchise model turns that scale into steady cash for shareholders. About 95% of its restaurants are run by franchisees who pay McDonald's rent and royalties, and it has raised its dividend for 50 straight years.

Industry observers note that what I like is how it keeps competing on value. Sales are still growing around the world, and in the U.S., where fewer customers had been walking in, sales turned positive in September after McDonald's pushed harder on value.

According to recent reports, to give lululemon its due, it has a premium brand and a new CEO working on a turnaround. But sales are shrinking, with North American shoppers buying less at existing stores, and the company cut its full-year outlook in its latest report.

According to recent reports, mcDonald's, by contrast, keeps paying shareholders steadily while it grows. For long-term investors, that mix of a trusted brand, steady cash, and a rising dividend makes McDonald's the better buy for 2027.

#119677. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4754 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • Recent findings suggest that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • These ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon confirmed his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

Recent findings suggest that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is crucial because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

Industry observers note that I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The firm’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company confirmed a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

Recent findings suggest that but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

In a recent development, such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. According to recent reports, claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. Sources indicate that an intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Industry observers note that pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

Recent findings suggest that there’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

Industry observers note that we cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

It has been revealed that A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s vital to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

It has been revealed that last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky rapidly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

According to recent reports, in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

According to recent reports, though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the manufacturer’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

Recent findings suggest that these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

It has been revealed that using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

Recent findings suggest that in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

It has been revealed that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Recent findings suggest that even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the organization judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

It has been revealed that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

In a recent development, what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

And that sprawling library isn't just about quantity, but quality, too, with content from major film studios including Paramount, MGM and Lionsgate, and television networks including A&E, Lifetime, and Starz.

According to recent reports, but to keep that platform feeling fresh and interesting, every once in a while Tubi has to say goodbye to some fan-favorite flicks and series to make room for a new wave of film and TV titles. And with another month rapidly coming to a close (where exactly did November go?), that means you'll have to act quickly if you want to catch these three great movies for $0 before they're gone.

Whether you're in the mood for a weepy autumnal favorite, a beloved Ben Stiller comedy, or a little dystopian trip back to Panem, here are three movies to stream before they leave Tubi soon.

Sources indicate that ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Blythe Danner, and Teri Polo are all back for a fourth "Meet the Parents" movie, "Focker in Law" — with the added fun of Ariana Grande playing a Focker daughter-in-law — which hits theaters nationwide on November 25. If you want to go back to the beginnings of the comedy franchise, though, the original "Meet the Parents" movie is available to watch on Tubi, but not for long.

If you missed the 2000 comedy all those years ago, "Meet the Parents" stars Stiller as the unfortunately-named Greg Focker, who is desperate to impress the parents of his girlfriend (Polo) during her sister's wedding, a goal made significantly more complicated by the fact that her dad is a formidable and overprotective CIA agent (De Niro).

Stream "Meet the Parents" on Tubi now.

Grab the Kleenex: It's "Stepmom" season. As she battles her illness, she must contend with her ex-husband's new partner, the much younger and career-driven Isabel Kelly (Julia Roberts), who will soon become the stepmother of Jackie's beloved children, Anna (Jena Malone) and Ben (Liam Aiken).

It has been revealed that but before you rush out to your nearest cinema, you can revisit the first installment in the Panem prequels, "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes," which is available to watch for free right now on Tubi. "Ballad" follows an 18-year-old Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth), who tries to restore his disgraced family's status in the post-war Capitol by mentoring Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), a tribute from the impoverished District 12. Stream "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" on Tubi now.

10 stocks we like better than Alibaba Group ›.

Industry observers note that investors looking for international growth often weigh the dominance of a Chinese tech leader against a global travel giant. Choosing between Alibaba Group (BABA -2.68%) and Booking Holdings (BKNG -1.64%) requires balancing valuation and regional risks.

In a recent development, alibaba operates a massive ecosystem of e-commerce and cloud services, leveraging its scale in the world's second-largest economy. Booking dominates the online travel industry by connecting millions of travelers with accommodations and services worldwide. While both companies benefit from digital transformation, they face distinct competitive and regulatory landscapes that will shape their paths toward 2027.

Alibaba focuses its strategy on the intersection of artificial intelligence and cloud computing alongside its core consumption platforms. The tech giant serves a vast merchant and consumer base through segments including China e-commerce, international digital commerce, and cloud intelligence. A key part of its strategy involves deepening customer loyalty, with its 88VIP membership base growing to approximately 64 million as of August 2026.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $160.3 billion, representing growth of approximately 5.5% compared to the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $17.6 billion during this same time frame. This growth reflects steady performance in its core commerce operations while it continues to invest in emerging cloud and international initiatives to capture long-term demand. (Alibaba reports in Chinese yuan. Figures have been converted to dollars at the exchange rate around the publication date.).

As of its March 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.2x, suggesting the organization uses a conservative amount of borrowed money relative to its own capital. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term debts with short-term assets, stood at nearly 1.3x. In the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, free cash flow was nearly negative $7.6 billion, meaning capital expenditures for the year exceeded the cash generated from operations.

One of the most prominent names among travel and tourism stocks, Booking provides online travel services through brands like Booking.com, Priceline, and Agoda. The company operates a global partner division that maintains commercial relationships with airlines, hotels, and rental car companies across 220 countries. Its primary strategy involves providing a seamless travel experience while leveraging massive consumer traffic derived from search engines and mobile app marketplaces.

For the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue grew by roughly 8% to reach about $28.1 billion. Net income for the period was approximately $7.2 billion, reflecting the high net margin associated with its asset-light business model. This performance demonstrates the tech giant's ability to capture resilient global travel demand even as it navigates a competitive landscape filled with diverse service providers.

Based on its December 2025 balance sheet, the company had a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly -3.5x. This negative value indicates that total liabilities exceed shareholder equity, a situation that often occurs in companies with significant share repurchases or specific financial structures. The current ratio was approximately 1.3x, while free cash flow reached about $9.1 billion in the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025.

Alibaba faces intense competition from established domestic rivals and emerging low-cost platforms that are challenging its market share in China. The manufacturer also operates in a complex regulatory environment that can shift rapidly, potentially affecting its cloud and financial technology interests. Geopolitical tensions may further complicate international expansion efforts and investor sentiment regarding its primary listing as it seeks to grow its global footprint.

Booking faces intense competition from global technology companies and travel providers like Airbnb (ABNB -1.41%) that use artificial intelligence to reach customers directly. The company is highly dependent on Alphabet Inc. (GOOG -2.59%) for traffic, where changes to search algorithms or latest AI features could increase the cost of acquiring customers. Regulatory compliance is also a major risk, particularly with European Union laws that impose operational restrictions and potential penalties on large digital platforms like those operated by Apple Inc. (AAPL -1.90%).

Alibaba trades at a lower valuation than Booking across both sales and future earnings estimates, though it carries different regional and regulatory risks.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Recent findings suggest that the P/S ratio measures the stock price against sales over the past twelve months. The Forward P/E ratio compares the current stock price to future earnings estimates for the coming year, helping investors understand how much they are paying for every dollar of projected profit.

In a recent development, booking Holdings is successfully shifting from an agency model to a primarily merchant model. That means it used to make its money as an agent--connecting travelers to a hotel and collecting a commission while the hotel manages collecting payment from the traveler. In the merchant model, Booking buys capacity from hotels and other providers on its platform and collects payment directly from the traveler. This tends to lead to fatter margins.

According to recent reports, the firm is also in excellent financial shape. It has $16 billion in cash, which makes its balance sheet investment grade. Another plus for shareholders is the company's $20 billion share buyback program. The brand is increasingly a destination for travelers, which means it is paying less to companies like Google for search engine visibility. Today, two-thirds of Booking.com's visitors are organic, meaning they are direct visitors rather than from paid ad traffic.

Sources indicate that revenue will grow about 9% this year to $29.3 billion. And net income takes a healthier 50% leap to about $8.1 billion.

It has been revealed that alibaba focuses on defending its cash-rich China e-commerce marketplaces, Taobao and Tmall, while funneling capital into higher-growth AI cloud and AI services. Alibaba is the public cloud leader in China and the owner of the Qwen open- and closed-source models. Yet its retail businesses are losing market share to Chinese rivals, which crimps the business's ability to fund money-losing AI model efforts. That means its AI cloud and compute services are the one impressive growth center for the business. It grew 45% year over year in that sector. One metric in its favor is that Alibaba's current valuation is attractive relative to U.S. cloud and AI peers.

Alibaba is forecast to continue growing, but some on the Street are skeptical of the manufacturer's ability to win in the hyper-competitive Chinese market and to expand its fast-growing AI services business beyond the China-dominated region, especially given the capital investment needed for AI.

BABA looks like a value play, but Booking is also priced below the average S&P 500 stock (which trades at a forward P/E of about 19x). And Booking's valuation is well below travel rival Airbnb. Yet the tech giant has robust total sales and good growth, expanding margins, and a pile of cash. It's too good a bargain to pass up at these prices. For 2027, go with Booking Holdings.

A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gpupartner

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen.
  • With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.
  • Industry observers note that openAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it.

With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.

Industry observers note that openAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience.

That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI: a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware.

According to recent reports, since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too.

Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times).

Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it.

Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list:.

In a recent development, that's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required.

It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations.

On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in.

Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster.

The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2.

It has been revealed that if you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable.

Recent findings suggest that for this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits.

According to recent reports, qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator. At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare.

If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs.

Industry observers note that if you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start.

RTX 5060 8GB, RTX 3060 12GB, RTX 5070 12GB.

Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE).

RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, RTX 5070 Ti, RTX 5080, RTX PRO 2000.

Gemma 4 31B, Qwen3.8-27B, Inkling 2 Mini.

RTX 3090, RTX 4090, RX 7900 XTX, RTX PRO 4000.

RTX 5090 32GB, RTX PRO 4500 32GB, RTX PRO 5000 48GB, RTX PRO 6000 96GB.

RTX 5060 8GB, RTX 3060 12GB, RTX 5070 12GB.

Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE).

RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, RTX 5070 Ti, RTX 5080, RTX PRO 2000.

Gemma 4 31B, Qwen3.8-27B, Inkling 2 Mini.

RTX 3090, RTX 4090, RX 7900 XTX, RTX PRO 4000.

RTX 5090 32GB, RTX PRO 4500 32GB, RTX PRO 5000 48GB, RTX PRO 6000 96GB.

Industry observers note that models marked MoE (mixture of experts) only run a few billion of their parameters for each token. They keep a decent speed on a smaller card with the rest held in system RAM, which is why a 35B model sits in the 16 GB row. On an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, our calculator puts Qwen3.6-35B at about 47 tokens per second this way.

Feel free to experiment with several models until you find one that fits your needs. You can also use GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator to get an estimate.

Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no.

Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context.

It has been revealed that nothing else in this guide changes. Revision Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2.

Those figures are Unsloth's. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower.

Inkling 2 Small is small in name only. It is a 594B model, and the smallest file Unsloth publishes is 171.7 GB. That is unified-memory territory: a 256GB Mac Studio or a DGX Station, not a graphics card.

According to recent reports, yes. You'll find good alternatives in Apple's Mac lineup thanks to its unified memory. Macs are pretty good at running larger models, even if they don't offer the best performance. Just make sure you grab the MLX flavor that is custom-built for Apple Silicon.

The same trade applies to unified-memory PCs like the MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ 11M and NVIDIA's DGX Spark.

It takes three steps: install Unsloth Desktop, download your model, and set the context size. I'll go over these steps in more detail below so you can follow along.

It has been revealed that first, we'll need a solution that 'serves' the AI model to you. My pursuit of simplicity narrowed my choices down to LM Studio or Unsloth Desktop. Both abstract away a ton of terminal commands and handle Python environments and dependencies behind a nice, simple UI, which makes them excellent picks for a first home setup.

Recent findings suggest that I landed on Unsloth Desktop mostly because, well, I liked the name better. Also, it didn't try to push the very thing I was trying to escape when I opened its website: a subscription.

The community seems to like it overall too, so that's another point in its favor.

Once you've clicked through the installer and launched Unsloth, you'll see a window like this one.

Unsloth Desktop on first launch, before any model is loaded.

Sources indicate that on the top left of this main window, you can pick the model that you want to use from the drop down. We'll be using Qwen3.8-27B.

It has been revealed that the model picker. Qwen3.8-27B is first on the Recommended list.

Sources indicate that you should see a submenu like the one below when you click on a model. I'll be using Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL version. The M and S versions are smaller, but the XL version behaves much closer to the full-size model without filling up our VRAM, so it seemed like a good pick for my GPU.

According to recent reports, every quantization of Qwen3.8-27B with its download size. The gear next to the downloaded one holds the context setting.

Once the download completes, you should see a gear icon to the right of the model as shown in the screenshot above. Here, you can set your context size manually or leave it on Auto if you aren't sure how much you need.

I'll be setting mine to 128K (unquantized) and might reassess after I've run the model through a few of my routine tasks for a few weeks. Again, you can use this VRAM calculator to help you with these numbers for your specific GPU.

At this point, our first local AI is up and running, and you can start chatting with it right inside Unsloth.

Remember, your mileage may vary depending on your setup.

It has been revealed that short answer: Unsloth Desktop has LAN sharing built in. Set a Remote password, start LAN access, and share the address it gives you with anyone on your home network.

Recent findings suggest that once Unsloth Desktop is set up with a model, you might want to give family members or friends access too. For now, we'll only serve it over our local network, so my family can use it without needing physical access to this PC.

Head into Unsloth Desktop settings (gear icon on bottom left), and look for the 'Remote & LAN' tab.

In a recent development, settings, Remote & LAN. LAN access is the second card. The Remote access card above it is for a later part.

Most of this section will be greyed out until you set a Remote password. Once you've set a password, you'll see a 'Start' button for LAN access. Click that and you should see an address that anyone on your home network can open in a browser to use a local AI model within a chat interface. They'll sign in as 'unsloth' with the Remote password you set.

Just keep in mind that the PC needs to stay on with Unsloth running for anyone to reach it.

Industry observers note that not with this setup alone. Everything so far is limited to your local home network.

If you just need a chat interface like ChatGPT, Gemini, etc. to work within your home network, you're basically done at this point! You and anyone on your network can start talking to an AI model hosted on your machine right away.

In a recent development, in the next parts, we'll cover performance, tunneling, as well as setting up an agent that runs locally and uses only the web tools you allow it to use. This will let you automate more complex tasks like coding, research, and so much more without being tied to a subscription or usage limits and censorship.

As always, my focus remains simplicity that allows my family to use it without too much guidance or help.

PS. If you have any recommendations for agentic harnesses or even models to try, feel free to let me know and I'll give them a go!

The Shokz OpenDots 2 aren't bone conduction, they hook onto side of your ear and then pipe tunes and podcasts directly into your ear. They're tiny, discreet, and they sound pretty good for something that doesn't go immediately into your ear canal. This $60 saving is a great way to grab a deal this Black Friday.

What These 6 Snack and Beverage Stocks Have in Common

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that investors who have been around the block know that when it comes to reducing risk and tapping into reliable dividends, some of the largest consumer-staples companies by market cap are excellent places to start.
  • These six beverage and snack stocks serve steady diets of delectable dividends.
  • For equity income investors, that's an extensive list from which to choose, and it's reasonable to ponder what these companies have in common besides residence in the consumer staples sector and the food and beverage industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Todd Shriber – Nov 22, 2026 at 2:17PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›.

Sources indicate that investors who have been around the block know that when it comes to reducing risk and tapping into reliable dividends, some of the largest consumer-staples companies by market cap are excellent places to start. That group includes Brown-Forman (BFB -0.66%) (BFA -0.74%), Coca-Cola (KO +0.94%), Hormel Foods (HRL +2.08%), J.M. Smucker (SJM +1.82%), PepsiCo (PEP +1.11%), and Sysco (SYY +1.32%).

These six beverage and snack stocks serve steady diets of delectable dividends. Image source: Getty Images.

For equity income investors, that's an extensive list from which to choose, and it's reasonable to ponder what these companies have in common besides residence in the consumer staples sector and the food and beverage industry.

The answer is easy and vital for dividend seekers: All six are at minimum Dividend Aristocrats®, members of the S&P 500 that have raised payouts for at least 25 consecutive years. (Dividend Aristocrats® is a registered trademark of Standard & Poor's Financial Services LLC.).

Let's examine each one from a dividend perspective.

Typically, the minimum age to open a U.S. brokerage account is 18, though some firms allow 13- to 17-year-olds to open an account with a parent or guardian. This means that younger investors can buy shares of Brown-Forman before they can legally enjoy the tech giant's products, including Jack Daniel's and Woodford Reserve, among other well-known liquor brands.

It has been revealed that the organization, which also makes Chambord liqueur and Diplomático rum, yields 3%, or nearly triple the S&P 500's dividend, and is on a 42-year run of consecutive annual dividend raises. If recent history is an accurate predictor, November could be the month in which Brown-Forman makes it 43 straight years of boosted payouts, so that's something to keep an eye on over the near term.

Industry observers note that something else long-term investors should monitor with Brown-Forman and related stocks is alcohol consumption trends among Gen Zers and millennials. Younger people are consuming slightly less alcohol today than they did during the worst part of the pandemic.

On the more positive side of the ledger for Brown-Forman is evidence suggesting that those consumers are being more selective when they do drink, indicating they are looking to trade up to premium brands, including some from the Brown-Forman stable.

Industry observers note that with payout increase streaks of 65 years and 55 years, respectively, soft drink giants Coca-Cola and PepsiCo are Dividend Kings -- companies that have raised dividends in at least 50 straight years. Yet, while the two share dividend growth, industry, and sector, these stocks' trajectories differ significantly. For the decade ended Nov. 13, Coke returned about 230% while PepsiCo gained 92%.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

This year, Coca-Cola, though a little frothy on valuation, is regularly printing newly introduced all-time highs while beating Pepsi stock by roughly 10 to 1. The latter is being pinched on multiple fronts, including tepid performance in the key North American market and sluggishness in its salty snacks division , a segment to which Coke is less exposed.

Both of these dividends are widely considered safe, but if "safe" is how investors want to play it, Coca-Cola has obvious momentum on its side. At the same time, PepsiCo is a "show me" story that may, in the near term, lack the clarity some market participants demand.

As noted above, there are concerns about the strength of PepsiCo's snacks unit, but those worries aren't uniform across the staples sector.

Industry observers note that just look at J.M. Smucker. In a sign that the fretting about weight-loss drugs hurting snack consumption may be misplaced, shares of this dividend growth star that is the maker of Twinkies are up 41% year to date. That's stellar among packaged-food stocks, and of note to prospective investors is that Smucker raised its full-year earnings guidance in August, saying it's having some success in passing higher costs on to consumers.

According to recent reports, hormel is a different story. While the company's Spam product found its way into post-Election Day discourse, shares of this Dividend King are slightly in the red this year. But there is hope for the maker of Pepperoni Bites and Planters nuts.

Management is known to be prudent with the balance sheet and is aware that the dividend is paramount to its investors. Some experts see Hormel's dividend growth over the next several years coming in at around 3% annually, which could keep pace with or beat inflation.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

As for Sysco -- a Dividend King in its own right that distributes snacks to an array of commercial clients -- the stock slipped following the fiscal first-quarter earnings report earlier this month as investors digested the dual specters of soft sales and higher costs.

That dip may be an opportunity because some analysts argue that the market is overreacting to one weak quarter while possibly ignoring Sysco's progress with deployment of artificial intelligence (AI). The food distributor could harness $100 million in 2027 savings from AI adoption, along with the organization's ability to scale up its food-service unit. Sysco shares yield 2.9%.

Shopping for a significant-screen TV on Black Friday? Check these 5 things first

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TV deals are one of the best parts of Black Friday, and if you’re vigilant, you’ve probably already noticed discounts starting to trickle in.
  • But making a significant purchase like a TV is also where a bad deal can cost you the most.
  • So, let’s not spoil your Thanksgiving dinner, and make sure you get the best TV deal you can this Black Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TV deals are one of the best parts of Black Friday, and if you’re vigilant, you’ve probably already noticed discounts starting to trickle in. If you’ve been eyeing a big-screen TV and waiting for your moment to strike, this is probably the best time of year to buy one.

But making a significant purchase like a TV is also where a bad deal can cost you the most. A huge discount can look great on paper, and it’s easy to miss the fine print when the low price tag grabs all your attention. You’ll save money now, but if you buy the wrong TV for you, you may find yourself annoyed months later when you realize you picked up a model with the wrong panel, weak gaming specs, or another personal deal-breaker.

So, let’s not spoil your Thanksgiving dinner, and make sure you get the best TV deal you can this Black Friday. Before you add anything to your cart, here are five things I’d check first.

If you're looking for a TV that delivers fast action and flawless detail, the UR8 RGB MiniLED TV from Hisense creates natural color that's closer to real life. Its AI processor will adjust the picture in real time, balancing it without any manual setup, so sunsets look warm and skin tones look natural. The 180Hz motion processing reduces blur so you can clearly see what's going on, whether it's in a fast-moving action movie or the latest AAA video game.

It has been revealed that when you start TV shopping, try not to get bogged down by the “was” price you’ll see in massive, bold letters on the product page. Instead, treat it as context. The “was” price is usually just the TV’s launch MSRP, and plenty of TVs sell for well below it for most of their shelf lives. What matters most is the current price compared to what the TV cost in September and October of 2026, so pull up a price tracker before you pull the trigger. If the deal doesn’t beat its most recent price, it isn’t really a deal.

Older models are also where a lot of the deepest discounts hide. Retailers still have last year’s stock to clear, and we’ve even noted that 2025 TVs may be the safer buy this year considering recent tech price hikes. Double-check what you’d give up by going with an older version. Sometimes it’s something inconsequential like a tiny bit of brightness. Or, sometimes it’s something you really care about, like a faster refresh rate for gaming.

Consider where you’ll actually put the TV before you buy it, because the room will determine the panel you need. OLED is always my pick for a dark room. But if your living room gets a lot of natural light, brightness and glare resistance will matter more, and that’s where Mini-LED shines. It gets brighter, usually costs less per inch, and some models have screens built to fight reflections. The anti-glare screen on the Hisense U6SF Pro I reviewed stood out.

According to recent reports, there’s a middle lane, too. QLED TVs are usually the budget-friendly option, with bright, punchy color for less money. The tradeoff is that they typically have fewer dimming zones than a Mini-LED, so blacks can look a bit grayer when you turn the lights down.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

As an avid gamer, this is the part of the spec sheet I read first. Look for native 120Hz or 144Hz panels, variable refresh rate (VRR), and the number of HDMI 2.1 ports. A TV can say “4K at 144Hz” and still offer only two HDMI 2.1 ports. That’s totally fine if you have just one or two gaming consoles. But toss in another device and a soundbar, and you’ll run out of room fast. So, take stock of all your gear first to figure out the configuration you need. If you can get a TV with four HDMI 2.1 ports, that’s pretty much the best-case scenario.

It has been revealed that while you’re at it, check the TV’s OS, too, since you’ll be using it to navigate your content every day. There’s no wrong choice between Roku, Fire TV (Vega OS), and Google TV, but if you’d rather not relearn a remote, it’s worth knowing which one comes in the box. Personally, I like Roku TVs for their streamlined simplicity, but your mileage may vary.

When it comes to TVs, the price tag is just the beginning. TV speakers are usually not great, and the bigger the screen is, the more you’ll notice. I’d strategy on snagging one of the best soundbars with pretty much any set. Make sure there’s room for it, though, because some TVs sit pretty low, and a soundbar can end up blocking the bottom of the picture or the sensor. Also, please don’t forget to measure your space. Make sure to check the TV stand width against your media console (lots of big TVs have feet way out at the edges), the doorway, and the wall if you’re mounting it.

It has been revealed that I’d also think twice about any extended warranty pitches at checkout. They aren’t always a bad idea, but check what the manufacturer’s warranty already includes first. While you’re at it, I’d also check the return window. Some retailers stretch theirs for the holidays, but some don’t, and January is a bad time to find that out.

It has been revealed that conventional wisdom states that TV prices bottom out around Black Friday and Cyber Monday, but this year comes with an asterisk. Chips and panels have both gotten pricier, and there aren’t many signs that will change anytime soon. That doesn’t mean prices won’t drop later this month, but it does mean the price floor might be a bit higher than you remember. So if a TV passes the first four checks and the price makes you happy, I’d buy it now. Holding out for another $100 off is how people end up missing out on the TV they really want.

My rule of thumb is to set a maximum price before I start scrolling, and set a price alert for the model(s) I want. It’ll keep the countdown timers and “only 3 left!” banners from making the final decision for you. Also, ask about the store’s price adjustment policy—some will refund the difference if the price drops within a set window.

It has been revealed that if you end up missing the best deal, don’t panic. Cyber Monday is right after Black Friday, and TVs often go on sale well into December. The catch is that popular sizes of the best models tend to sell out first. Ultimately, the best Black Friday TV deal is the one that best fits your room and budget.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that one of Apple’s most beloved products this year was undoubtedly the MacBook Neo. Unlike some of its other budget products, Apple seems interested in updating the MacBook Neo on an annual cycle, and we may get the next MacBook Neo around March.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is targeting the iOS/macOS 27.4 release cycle for the release of the new MacBook Neo, as well as the A19 budget iPad, iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and OLED iPad Air.

While he notes that this cycle runs between February and March, it doesn’t necessarily mean the products will launch on the earlier end of that spectrum. Apple is also expected to release the iPhone Air 2, OLED iPad Air, and a newly introduced iPad Pro within the first half of the year, but they’ll likely come a bit later than the aforementioned products.

As expected, the next MacBook Neo will bump up from the A18 Pro chip with 8GB of RAM to the A19 Pro chip with 12GB of RAM.

It has been revealed that apple will also introduce upcoming colors on the MacBook Neo “frequently,” though it’s unclear if we’ll see that with the next iteration. From the Power On newsletter:.

In a recent development, the other thing I’ve heard is that Apple plans to refresh the MacBook Neo’s colors frequently. We’ll see if that trend starts with the first follow-up.

Recent findings suggest that I’m certainly excited to see the next generation MacBook Neo, especially with 12GB of unified memory. While 8GB is certainly fine, heavy multitaskers will notice it, especially with unoptimized software.

The bigger question is: will the next MacBook Neo have a price increase? With additional RAM included, it feels inevitable.

Apple increased the price of MacBook Neo from $599 to $699 back in June, and in October the manufacturer also silently decreased the education discount by $50, meaning the education price has increased from $499 to $649 since launch.

If there is a price increase, it likely won’t be too major, maybe $50 – leaving the computer at $749. Compared to the rest of the laptop landscape, MacBook Neo would still be a good value. We’ll see what happens.
